questions.question: Comprehension: Read the following passage and answer the questions given after it. In a kingdom veiled in antiquity, resided a queen bereft of progeny. The heavens had withheld the gift of a child, leaving the queen in constant prayer within her garden, seeking divine benevolence for a child. One morning, an angel traversed the heavenly realms to relay God’s message—she would bear a son, endowed with the power of wishing, granting him the ability to conjure anything. Joy blossomed within her, and she shared the blessed news with the king, whose heart swelled with happiness at the birth of their son. The queen, accompanied by her child, would often visit the garden, cleansing themselves in a crystalline stream amongst the beasts. One such morning, the queen, entrapped in slumber’s embrace, was deceived by the malevolent cook, aware of the child's extraordinary gift. He snatched the child, stained the queen’s apparel with hen’s blood, and secreted the child away, accusing the queen of neglect. The perceived betrayal drove the king to imprison his wife within a sunlight-deprived tower for seven years, awaiting her slow demise. Divine intervention manifested as two doves, nourishing her with heavenly food. Fearing retribution, the cook abandoned the palace and manipulated the growing prince to wish for luxurious possessions and a companion, a girl of unparalleled beauty. Their bonds of companionship tightened, inducing the cook’s fear of the prince seeking his real father. The malevolent cook demanded the maiden to assassinate the prince. Her refusal to comply led to the subterfuge of presenting a hind’s heart and tongue as those of the prince. Meanwhile, the prince condemned the cook into a perpetual torment of consuming burning coals as a black poodle. Yearning for his mother, the prince, the maiden transformed into a pink, and the dog-cook traveled back to his kingdom. The prince’s power revealed his mother's pitiable existence, provoking the revelation of his true identity and the cook’s sinister machinations during a royal feast. The malevolent cook returned to his human form, his crimes exposed, and the innocent queen finally freed, albeit her life dwindling rapidly, fueled by years of anguish. The king, mired in grief and regret, met his demise shortly after witnessing the cook’s just punishment, his body quartered.
